hook.line: Everyone in La Candelaria has a story about how Rosa became the best-known name on the block. It did not happen overnight, and Spanish has a phrase for that long road.
hook.es: Rosa llegó a ser la dueña del café.
hook.en: Rosa ended up becoming the owner of the café.

examples.es: Rosa llegó a ser la dueña del café.
examples.en: Rosa ended up becoming the owner of the café.

examples.es: Hernando llegó a ser el taxista más conocido del barrio.
examples.en: Hernando became the best-known taxi driver in the neighborhood.

examples.es: Llegó a ser una de las científicas más reconocidas del país.
examples.en: She became one of the country's best-known scientists.

examples.es: Llegué a pensar que no volvería.
examples.en: I got to the point of thinking he wouldn't come back.

examples.es: Llegamos a creer que el café cerraría.
examples.en: We came to believe the café would close.

rule:
*Llegar a ser* + a noun or adjective means "to become" after a long road: years of work, luck, time. It is for the big results.

*Llegó a ser directora.*

You will usually see it in the past. Add *no* and it means someone never made it: *No llegó a ser famosa*.

The same *llegar a* + infinitive means "to get to the point of", usually with thinking or feeling: *llegué a pensar*, *llegamos a creer*.

For a quick change, *llegar a ser* is too heavy. Use *estaba nervioso*, not "I arrived at being nervous".
smallPrint: Teachers call this a verb of change (*verbo de cambio*), the slow, effortful kind.

readAndPick.es: Rosa llegó a ser la dueña del café.
options: Rosa wanted to be the owner of the café.
Rosa arrived at the owner of the café.
Rosa ended up becoming the owner of the café.

readAndPick.es: Rosa llegó al café a las ocho.
options: Rosa arrived at the café at eight.
Rosa became the café at eight.
Rosa ended up owning the café at eight.

readAndPick.es: Llegué a pensar que no volvería.
options: I arrived thinking he wouldn't come back.
I got to the point of thinking he wouldn't come back.
I thought he would never leave.
She never became famous.
She became famous.
She didn't want to be famous.

readAndPick.es: Hernando llegó a ser el taxista más conocido del barrio.
options: Hernando wanted to be the best-known taxi driver.
Hernando became the best-known taxi driver in the neighborhood.
Hernando arrived at the taxi driver's neighborhood.
They became very well known.
She became very well known.
They arrived well known.

readAndPick.es: Llegamos a creer que el café cerraría.
options: We want to believe the café will close.
We arrived believing the café would close.
We came to believe the café would close.
I got to the point of hating that car.
I arrived in that car hating it.
I always loved that car.

yourTurn.prompt: Say "Rosa became the owner of the café." Choose *a ser* or *ser*, then type it: *Rosa llegó ___ la dueña del café.*
yourTurn.answer: Rosa llegó a ser la dueña del café.
yourTurn.why: The frame always has *a*: *llegó a ser*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "Vale became the best cook in Medellín."
yourTurn.answer: Vale llegó a ser la mejor cocinera de Medellín.
yourTurn.why: *Llegó a ser* + the noun, with *la mejor* for "the best".

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "I came to think he wouldn't come back."
yourTurn.answer: Llegué a pensar que no volvería.
accept: Llegué a pensar que él no volvería.
yourTurn.why: With thoughts, *llegar a* + infinitive means "got to the point of".

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "We came to believe the café would close."
yourTurn.answer: Llegamos a creer que el café cerraría.
yourTurn.why: For "we" it is *llegamos a*, then the infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it plural, about several women: *Llegó a ser muy conocida.*
yourTurn.why: The verb takes *-ron* and the adjective takes *-s*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative, "she never became famous": *Llegó a ser famosa.*
yourTurn.why: *No llegó a ser* says she never made it.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "I got to the point of hating that car."
yourTurn.why: Feelings work like thoughts: *llegué a* + infinitive.

pitfalls.why: Almost. English "became" is one word, but Spanish always puts *a* before *ser*.
Close. Without *ser*, *llegó a* just means she arrived somewhere.

pitfalls.wrong: Llegué a ser nervioso antes de la entrevista.
pitfalls.right: Estaba nervioso antes de la entrevista.
pitfalls.why: *Llegar a ser* is for a long road, not for a quick change like getting nervous.

personal: Say what you would like to end up becoming, or what a friend ended up becoming: *Llegó a ser...* or *Quiero llegar a ser...*.
